data.description: Santa Clara County has decided to stop using Flock Safety cameras in several cities due to privacy concerns.

City council voted unanimously to reject the $666,000 contract extension with Flock Safety after public pushback and concerns over privacy, civil liberties, and sharing data with federal agencies. Despite their vote, Mayor Johnston went behind council's back and negotiated 2 deals with Flock Safety to keep them in town.

City council voted to block the renewal of Austin\'s contract with Flock Safety after controversial uses for the system, violations of department policy, and contract language that went against council mandates on data retention.
City council voted to cancel its contract with Flock Safety following a state investigation of the system\'s data sharing practices, which enabled violations of state law.

The City of Evanston ended its contract with Flock Safety and requested the deactivation of the cameras following an audit by the Secretary of State showing the company was violating state law by sharing Illinois data with federal agencies. Flock then reinstalled the cameras against the city's wishes, prompting a cease-and-desist by the city.
The City of Louisville deactivated its cameras after a community member found that the system was severely misrepresented in both its data sharing practices and its capabilities.
City council voted unanimously to end their contract with Flock Safety after council members claimed they were misled and lied to about the system's data sharing features.

City council voted 6-1 to reject a contract with Flock Safety after an overwhelmingly negative public response, citing privacy concerns, government overreach, poor use of taxpayer money, and concerns with data sharing.
Following a pause by City Council, Eugene PD eventually terminated their contract with Flock Safety.
The City of Stanwood decided to shut off its Flock cameras pending a court judgment on whether data collected by Flock cameras are considered public records.
City council voted against a contract with Flock Safety after community members raised concerns about privacy, civil liberties, and data sharing.
The Elbert County Board of County Commissioners unanimously voted not to renew its contract with Flock Safety after concerns of government overreach.
City council voted unanimously to reject a contract with Flock Safety after hearing community concerns about privacy, civil liberties, and data sharing with federal agencies.
The Village of Scarsdale terminated its contract with Flock Safety after over 450 community members signed a petition, expressing concerns over privacy and the system's data sharing practices.
Hays County commissioners voted 3-2 to terminate their contract with Flock Safety after public concern for privacy and the risk of their personal information being exposed.
The Town of Warrenton voted 5-1 to permanently block consideration of installing ALPRs in their town.

The Redmond city council voted unanimously to request the police department to disable their Flock cameras after growing concerns of unwanted access by federal agencies and a recent WA court ruling that ALPR data is considered public record.
The Kent city council voted against a Flock contract due to concerns of potential abuse and discomfort with mass surveillance.
Olympia City Council moved to cover up their Flock cameras, pending deactivation over concerns of federal access and the ability to move freely.
Lane County, Oregon suspended their contract with Flock Safety, before their 22 cameras were even installed due to public opposition.
Following Eugene's lead, Springfield terminated their contract with Flock Safety, after strong community opposition.
Flagstaff City Council voted unanimouslt and to end their contract with Flock Safety, following failed attempts to convince the public that sufficient guardrails could be put in place.
Cambridge ended its contract with Flck Safety following a "breach of trust" in which Flock installed new cameras without the city's knowledge following a temporary suspension by the city.

The Walla Walla Police Department disabled its Flock system due to concerns that the data from them could be misused, following a Washington court ruling that data captured by Flock cameras were public records and could be requested by anyone.

The Los Altos Hills City Council voted to terminate their contract with Flock Safety (2:45:02) following resident concerns and a lack of evidence that the Flock system was effective at reducing crime.
The Santa Cruz City Council voted 6-1 to terminate their contract with Flock Safety after evidence that the city's data was accessed by out-of-state agencies.
The Lynnwood Police Department paused the used of their Flock system following concerns raised by residents.
Woodburn, Oregon announced they would pause the use of their Flock system following safety concerns for undocumented residents.
The town of Hillsborough, North Carolina terminated their contract with Flock Safety following concerns about data privacy.
The town of Warren, Rhode Island rejected a proposal to install Flock LPRs due to concerns about privacy violations.
The Mountlake Terrace City Council voted unanimously to cancel their contract with Flock Safety following concerns of data access and public records implications.
Richmond's police chief shut down the city's Flock system after discoving their data was unintentionally being shared nationwide.
The Staunton Police Chief and City Council canceled their contract with Flock Safety following a verbal attack on the city's residents by the CEO of Flock.

The Charlottesville City Council decided not to move forward with a contract with Flock Safety following the conclusion of their pilot program, due to their concerns with the system outweighing any benefits.
The Bay City Commission voted against a contract with Flock Safety following community members expressing privacy concerns.
The San Marcos City Council voted to end their contract with Flock Safety after considering Flock's reputaiton.
Sedro-Woolley deactivated their Flock cameras following a lawsuit resulting in Flock footage being considered public records under Washington state law.
Bend City Council voted to deactivate and remove their Flock cameras over concerns with Flock's business practices.
Lake County commissioners ordered Flock to remove their cameras following their illegal and unpermitted installation, a tactic by Flock that still occurs in 2026.
Watertown, MA canceled its contract with Flock Safety before any cameras were installed, following questions from the public about privacy and data sharing.

The town of Natick canceled their Flock Safety pilot after residents objected to being blindsided by the installation and raised privacy and surveillance concerns. The police launched the trial without notifying the Select Board or public, triggering backlash over transparency, data ownership, and mass surveillance risks, leading to cameras being slated for removal.
Prosser disabled their Flock cameras due to the controversial issues of data collection an access.
The Verona City Council voted not to renew their contract with Flock Safety after concerns about data access.
Flock cameras were deactivated in Knoxville, TN following a contract lapse. However, the city intends to pursue a contract with another vendor.
The Mountain View Police Chief decided to disable their Flock cameras after noticing their cameras had been accessed by out-of-state and federal agencies, a violation of California law.
Brooklyn Park canceled their Flock contract “due to concerns over customer support and poor data sharing protocols.”
Skamania County stopped using Flock Safety cameras after a Washington court ruled the images captured by them were public records and could be requested by anyone.
The Seneca Police Department ended its contract with Flock license plate readers after less than 90 days, citing poor customer service and security concerns.

UPDATE: Everett has rejoined the Flock after WA state passed a law exempting ALPR data - including audit logs - from FOIA. The City of Everett shut down its entire network of Flock license plate reader cameras after a judge ruled the footage is considered public record.
Oxnard police suspended operation of its 19 Flock fixed-position cameras after a vendor error allowed out-of-state agencies to query local data.
Ithica Common Council ended the city’s contract with Flock Safety due to privacy concerns.
Saranac Lake, NY canceled its contract with Flock following public outcry and concerns over privacy.
The Dutchtown Community Improvement District ended its contract with Flock Safety amid concerns over data-sharing with ICE.
Sturgeon Bay will discontinue using the Flock System after overwhelming opposition was voiced by the public
Bloominton, IN terminated its $50,000 contract with Flock Safety after 400+ residents protested the surveillance system.
Salem, IL canceled an earlier agreement for use of Flock license reader cameras due to a change in contract terms that were concerning to the Mayor.
Dane County, WI cut off funding for Flock cameras due to privacy concerns.
Tompkins County, NY ended the county’s contract with Flock Safety after months of organized pushback from activists and community members.
The City of South Tucson, AZ canceled their contract with Flock Safety, removing the automated license plate reader cameras after months of debate over privacy and public safety.
The Oshkosh Common Council rescinded its approval of the Flock camera contract just one day after it was initially approved.
The city of Ypsilanti, MI voted to ban license plate readers, citing privacy concerns.
Shoreline, WA rejected the possibility of a contract with Flock Safety due to public opposition and concerns among council members.
The El Cerrito city council voted not to renew its contract with Flock; the cameras will be turned off on June 7.
Appleton's mayor announced that the city will stop using Flock due to community feedback and concerns over the integrity of the system.
The Pittsboro town board voted 4-1 to cancel its contract for the controversial system of license-plate readers, siding with privacy rights.
The City of Weston has removed its Flock cameras after major pushback from residents.
City council unanimously voted down a proposed contract with Flock Safety, rejecting the activation of Flock Cameras in the city, and also voted to cancel their existing contract.
South Portland City Council voted to stop using Flock cameras due to concerns over data security and privacy.
Fort Collins canceled its contract with Flock Safety, ending the city's participation in the automated license plate reader system.
City council voted to end the Flock Safety camera contract.
Framingham will not renew its contract with Flock Safety, ending the city’s use of the company’s automated license plate reader camera system after months of public debate.
The City of Bishop terminated a five-year contract with Flock Safety after residents expressed concerns about privacy violations and data searches.
The Ashland Police Department decided to not renew its contract for Flock Safety cameras as their one-year agreement has expired.
Bandera city council terminated the city’s contract with Flock Safety Systems following public opposition to the planned license plate reader camera program.
The Monona Police Department decided not to renew its contract for Flock Safety's automated license plate reader system.
The City of Fitchburg discontinued their contract with Flock Safety due to privacy concerns and cost.

The McFarland Police Department will not move forward with a planned purchase of automated license plate reader technology from Flock Safety following decisions by neighboring agencies to stop using it.
The University of Wisconsin-Madison Police Department will remove automated license plate reader cameras from campus after ending its contract with Flock Safety.
Sheriff Brian Craig stated that the Flock cameras will be removed once the contract expires at the end of August. the cameras will be removed.
Mount Vernon has turned off the city’s Flock cameras following a vote by the council on June 24.
Killingworth will soon end its contract with Flock Safety for automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras due to funding issues and concerns about privacy.
The Flock camera contract for Westland will not be renewed following community feedback.
The Los Angeles Police Department is ending its agreement with surveillance company Flock Safety.
Green River city council rejected a $111,956 grant for automated license plate readers due to public opposition, by a vote of 6-1.
Kaukauna chose not to renew its contract with Flock Safety due to growing privacy concerns.
Newport has decided to remove Flock cameras from the city after receiving feedback from residents.
Macon county's Flock Safety license plate reader camera program was defunded after a unanimous vote by commissioners.
Windsor ended their contract with Flock Safety due to concerns over privacy and data management.
Syracuse has removed all of its 13 license plate readers from city property.
The Clearwater County Sherriff's Office will not renew its agreement for the Flock camera system after determining it did not provide enough operational value.
Salem, MA will be removing the Flock cameras that are currently installed.
Pea Ridge dropped Flock license plate readers after resident complaints about their use.
Elkton has cut ties with Flock Safety, effective immediately, following efforts by deflockthevalley.com.
The county canceled their contract with Flock Safety a year before it was set to expire.
Stoughton, WI city council voted to terminate their surveillance contract with Flock just seven months into a two-year term following community backlash over privacy concerns.
Harrisonburg honored its pledge and has ended the contract with Flock Safety in a unanimous vote.
Taos defunded the contract with Flock Safety, terminating the use of 18 AI surveillance cameras.
Kingstown, RI has canceled their contract with Flock Safety, although the company's hardware may still appear along state routes under a contract with RI state police.
Ord city council voted 5-0 to remove their Flock cameras in response to residents' privacy concerns.
A unanimous vote led to the cancelation of Narragansett's contract with Flock Safety, more than a year before it was set to expire.
The Centerton City Council voted to terminate their contract with Flock, following concerns over privacy and public opinion.
Mayflower has discontinued their use of Flock Safety license plate readers, citing concerns about privacy.
The Winona Police Department announced it has opted not to replace Flock cameras in the city.
Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teepleannounced the cancellation of their contract with Flock, citing 4th amendment concerns.
The new Garden City police chief stated he is not willing to invest in LPRs at this time.
Sheriff Joshua Ray terminated the contract with Flock Safety following a unanimous vote by the Commissioners Court.
Lago Vista City Council voted unanimously to remove their Flock camera after residents raised concerns about privacy and oversight.
Eagle Sports Range removed the Flock cameras from their parking lot amid privacy concerns raised by a viral video, despite threats from Flock about their contractual obligations.
The Duluth Police Department will not be renewing their 12-month grant-funded contract with Flock.
The Josephine County Sheriff's Office canceled their contract with Flock cameras amid public concerns regarding privacy and vandalism.
Waukee is not renewing its contract with Flock Safety.
The city of Surprise canceled its contract with Flock Safety following the discovery of an 'anomaly' during a routine audit.
Littleton police announced they have fully disabled the Flock cameras in town, with four physically removed and the remaining two scheduled for removal in September.
The Coshocton County Sheriff’s Office decided to remove all Flock Safety cameras in response to concerns raised by local residents regarding privacy and state surveillance.
Sherburne County has discontinued its services agreement with Flock Safety, disabled camera search capabilities, and began the process of removing the cameras, in order to preserve public trust.
Coweta Police Chief Mike Bell has announced plans to unplug the town’s two Flock Safety cameras due to community concerns about privacy and trust in the police department.
The Salida Police Department is canceling their contract with Flock due to community concerns about privacy and civil liberties.
The Henry County Sheriff's Office will not renew its contract with Flock Safety amid growing privacy concerns.
Hood County has shut down and covered Flock cameras over privacy concerns raised by county commissioners and residents.
The Pulaski County Sheriff's Office announced that it will not renew its Flock contract nor pursue another vendor, due to public concerns about privacy and surveillance.

The Winston, OR Police Department has ended its contract with Flock amid budget cuts and privacy concerns. "... If they [the citizens] don’t want them, we’re going to turn them off," said Police Chief Brandon Sarti.
Indianola deactivated its Flock cameras to review privacy concerns raised by the community.
The city of Fort Mitchell will end the use of Flock cameras following community concerns.
Whandot County has begun removing Flock cameras after resident feedback.
The Bolivar Board of Aldermen will terminate the city's contract with Flock, following concerns from constituents regarding privacy.
The Sullivan County Sheriff's Office suspended the use of license plate reader cameras due to ongoing threats and public controversy.
A controversial surveillance camera pointed at a Madison Heights cannabis dispensary has been taken down as the result of a new agreement between the city and the company.
East Bridgewater police department will terminate its contract with Flock due to privacy concerns of residents.
Marietta City Council canceled its contract for Flock license plate reader cameras after residents raised concerns about privacy and data retention.
The Grafton Police Department has begun the process of deactivating all Flock devices amid growing concerns about the use of this technology in the community.
The West Salem Police Department removed its five Flock cameras due to cost and limited use, stating that it would not be fiscally responsible to continue the program without community funding.
The Wellsville Police Department terminated all agreements with Flock following concerns expressed by the community.
Lansing city council adopted a resolution to end all contracts with Flock.
Douglas, Mass will discontinue their use of Flock cameras.
The Davidson County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to remove all 25 of the sheriff's department’s Flock cameras.
Sheriff Allen announced he is ending all three contracts the county has with Flock due to concerns over data privacy.
City council denied the Fort Wayne Police Department's use of more than $120,000 for Flock cameras.
The Town of Cave Creek has terminated its agreement with Flock due to resident concerns and privacy limitations.
Lincoln County will stop using Flock cameras as announced by Sheriff René King.
Pflugerville canceled their contract with Flock, citing concerns about privacy and data protection.
Tempe ended their contract with Flock and turned off its cameras due to privacy concerns.
Pasco County is terminating their agreement with Flock and disallowing the operation of LPRs including Flock and Axon on public ROWs.
Sheboygan will request termination of the city's contract with Flock, and has begun bagging the cameras until they can be removed.
The Wylie City Council voted unanimously not to renew its contract with Flock, leading to the shutdown of its automated license plate reader cameras.
The Giles County Sheriff’s Office will end its use of Flock cameras citing public concerns about data integrity.
Galva will stop using Flock cameras, following in the footsteps of the Henry County Sheriff's Office and in response to concerns about privacy and public trust.
The Lincoln County Sheriff announced the county will no longer use Flock cameras after strong opposition from community members.
The Christiansburg Town Council voted unanimously to remove their Flock cameras following privacy concerns from residents.
The city of Grants is terminating its agreement with Flock due to concerns that the benefits did not align with the city's mission.
The city plans to deactivate its Flock LPRs immediately, citing community trust issues after receiving feedback regarding privacy concerns.
The Oceana County road commission revoked the right of way permits allowing several ALPRs to be installed, and the Sheriff's Office has canceled their pilot program.
The Greenville Police Department decided not to move forward with the planned implementation of the Flock system following feedback from residents and city leadership.
The Franklin County Board of Commissioners voted not to renew the county's contract with Flock due to concerns about data retention and privacy.
